body:
## Summary

Two weak PRNG usages in `src/core/core.cpp` could allow an attacker to predict which bootstrap nodes and TCP relays the client selects.

## Details

### `rand()` for TCP relay port selection (line 364)

```cpp
const auto tcpPort = dhtServer.tcpPorts[rand() % ports];
```

`rand()` is never seeded in this code, uses global state (not thread-safe), and is trivially predictable. A proper RNG (`std::mt19937`) is already initialized at line 44 but is not used here.

### Clock-seeded `mt19937` for bootstrap node shuffle (line 44)

```cpp
std::mt19937 rng(std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count());
```

The seed is the current time, which is predictable if the attacker knows the approximate startup time. This enables targeted Eclipse attacks where the attacker positions malicious DHT nodes to be selected first.

Same pattern in `src/ipc.cpp:80` for IPC `globalId` generation.

## Suggested Fix

Use cryptographically secure random sources:

```cpp
// Option 1: std::random_device
std::mt19937 rng(std::random_device{}());

// Option 2: Qt's secure RNG
const auto tcpPort = dhtServer.tcpPorts[QRandomGenerator::global()->bounded(ports)];
```

For the bootstrap shuffle (where the risk is lower since the node list is public), `std::random_device` seeding is sufficient. For the IPC globalId, consider using `QRandomGenerator::securelySeeded()`.

## Impact

An attacker who knows the approximate startup time can predict which bootstrap nodes and TCP relays the client tries first, facilitating Eclipse attacks on the DHT.
title: Predictable PRNG: `rand()` for TCP port, clock-seeded `mt19937` for bootstrap shuffle
